title: Fixed-horizon labels and their problems
objectives: Label returns over a fixed horizon and find its weaknesses.
Scale a dead zone by recent volatility and check the class balance.

screens.title: The fixed-horizon label in code
screens.prose: What you did has a name: the **fixed-horizon label** $y_t = \operatorname{sign}(P_{t+h}/P_t - 1)$. It is the `forward_label` alignment from validation lesson 7. Row $t$ holds what happens after $t$, and the last $h$ rows are dropped.
screens.question: Complete `fixed_horizon_label` so it returns one label per day that has a close $h$ days later.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: the twelve closes above and two tiny series, one with a flat day. The rest use a seeded series from `make_prices(750, seed=21)`, which is already defined. Lists must match exactly. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: With NumPy, `p[h:]` lines up each close with the one $h$ days before it, `p[:-h]`.
Both slices have length `len(p) - h`, which is exactly the number of labels.
Write `fwd = p[h:] / p[:-h] - 1`.

feedback.correct: One label per day with a future close; a flat day gets 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the length first: `len(prices) - h` labels.

explain.text: `p[h:] / p[:-h]` divides each close by the one $h$ days earlier, so entry $t$ is the move after day $t$. `np.sign` gives $+1$, $-1$, or $0$ for an exact tie, the edge case in the second test. With $h = 1$ the label is tomorrow's direction.

screens.title: A dead zone that scales
screens.prose: The fix: measure recent volatility $\sigma$, the sd of the last 20 daily returns. A five-day return has spread about $\sigma\sqrt{5}$. Label $0$ when $|R| \le k\sigma\sqrt{h}$. Here $\sigma = 1.8\%$, $h = 5$ and $k = 0.5$.
screens.question: Tap every return that is labelled $0$.

hints.text: Work out the threshold $k\sigma\sqrt{h}$ first.
$\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$. The close calls are these two.
$0.5 \times 1.8 \times 2.236 = 2.01\%$. Everything between $-2.01\%$ and $2.01\%$ is $0$.

feedback.correct: The bar is 2.01%, so −1.6%, +0.4% and +1.9% are labelled 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $0.5 \times 1.8\% \times \sqrt{5}$, then keep the returns inside it.

byKey.no-root: You used $k\sigma = 0.9\%$, a one-day bar. A five-day return spreads $\sqrt{5}$ times wider, so the bar is 2.01%.
byKey.root-two: You rounded $\sqrt{5}$ to 2, giving a bar of 1.8%. With $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236$ the bar is 2.01%, so +1.9% is inside it.
byKey.e: +2.3% is beyond the 2.01% bar, so it is $+1$.
byKey.a: −3.1% is beyond the bar, so it is $-1$.
byKey.f: +4.0% is beyond the bar, so it is $+1$.

explain.text: The bar is $0.5 \times 1.8\% \times \sqrt{5} = 2.01\%$. Three returns fall inside and get $0$; the rest keep their sign. In a calm month $\sigma$ shrinks and the bar shrinks with it.

screens.title: The dead-zone label in code
screens.prose: Now in code, on daily log returns, so an $h$-day return is a plain sum. Row $t$ may use returns up to $t$ for $\sigma$; the label uses $t + 1$ to $t + h$. The first `vol_window - 1` rows have no $\sigma$ yet, and the last $h$ have no future.
screens.question: Complete `dead_zone_label` so it returns $-1$, $0$ or $+1$ for every row that has both a $\sigma$ and a future.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def dead_zone_label(returns, h, vol_window, k):
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    labels = []
    for t in range(vol_window - 1, len(r) - h):
        sigma = r[t - vol_window + 1:t + 1].std(ddof=1)
        fwd = r[t + 1:t + h + 1].sum()
        thr = k * sigma * np.sqrt(h)
        labels.append(1 if fwd > thr else (-1 if fwd < -thr else 0))
    return labels

screens.title: How balanced are the labels?
screens.prose: Before training anything, count the classes. The three-year series from earlier drifted upwards, so we expect more $+1$ than $-1$. A share of each class is the first number to report.
screens.question: Complete `label_balance` so it returns the shares of $-1$, $0$ and $+1$, in that order, rounded to 4 places.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def label_balance(labels):
    y = np.asarray(labels)
    return [...]   # shares of -1, 0 and +1, each rounded to 4 places
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def label_balance(labels):
    y = np.asarray(labels)
    return [round(float(np.mean(y == c)), 4) for c in (-1, 0, 1)]

screens.title: The fixed-horizon family
screens.prose: With $R_t = P_{t+h}/P_t - 1$ and $\sigma_t$ the recent daily volatility, known at $t$: $$y_t = \begin{cases} +1 & R_t > k\sigma_t\sqrt{h} \\ 0 & |R_t| \le k\sigma_t\sqrt{h} \\ -1 & R_t < -k\sigma_t\sqrt{h} \end{cases}$$ With $k = 0$ this is the plain sign label. The last $h$ rows have no label.
screens.question: With $h = 1$, $k = 0$ and a close exactly unchanged, what is the label?

options.text: $0$: the return is exactly zero
$+1$, because the share did not fall
options.why: You counted "not down" as up. `np.sign(0)` is 0, and the case $|R| \le 0$ catches it.

options.text: No label: the row is dropped
options.why: Only rows with no future close are dropped. This row has one; its return is just zero.

hints.text: Put $R_t = 0$ into the cases.

feedback.correct: A flat close sits in the middle case even with no dead zone.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $R_t = 0$ and $k = 0$ into the three cases.

explain.text: With $k = 0$ the middle case reads $|R_t| \le 0$, which holds only for an exact zero. On prices quoted to the penny a flat close happens, so a binary label must decide where it goes. Our code gives it 0, a third class.

screens.title: A 55% hit rate
screens.prose: A research note claims a 55% hit rate on 1,000 one-day sign calls. Its appendix splits them. Moves under 0.1% (average size 0.05%): 600 calls, 350 right. Moves over 0.1% (average size 1.0%): 400 calls, 200 right. Each trade costs 0.10% round trip.
screens.question: What is the average return per trade after costs, in per cent?

widget.label: Average net return per trade, in per cent

hints.text: Right calls earn the move; wrong calls lose it. Net out each row.
Gross: $100 \times 0.05\% / 1000 = 0.005\%$ per trade. Subtract the 0.10% cost.

feedback.correct: About −0.095% a trade: the 55% came from moves too small to pay for themselves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each call by the size of its move, then subtract the cost.

byKey.gross: That is the gross return, 0.005% a trade. Each trade still pays 0.10%.
byKey.hit: You turned the 5-point edge in hit rate into 0.10% a trade. The edge sits on 0.05% moves, so it is worth far less.

explain.text: The edge lives in the small moves: 100 net right calls of 0.05% each; the big moves are a coin. After 0.10% per trade the strategy loses 0.095% a trade. Level 3 returns to costs; a label with a dead zone would never have counted those small calls.

ideas: The fixed-horizon label is the sign of the $h$-day forward return; the last $h$ rows have no label.
It labels tiny moves as confidently as big ones and ignores the path. It means different things in calm and wild markets.
A dead zone of $k\sigma\sqrt{h}$, with $\sigma$ known at $t$, keeps a label's meaning steady; then check the class balance.

summary.trap: A threshold fixed in per cent is a high bar in calm markets and a low one in wild markets.

quiz.prose: Fixed-horizon labels with $h = 5$ on consecutive days. Day $t$'s label uses the returns of days $t + 1$ to $t + 5$.
quiz.question: What share of day $t + 1$'s five returns does it share with day $t$'s label?

feedback.correct: Four of the five days are the same.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the days each label covers.

byKey.none: Neighbouring labels are not separate. Day $t + 1$ covers days $t + 2$ to $t + 6$.
byKey.one: One day is new, so four of five are shared: 80%.

explain.text: Day $t$ covers $t + 1$ to $t + 5$; day $t + 1$ covers $t + 2$ to $t + 6$. Four of five days are shared, so neighbouring labels nearly always agree. Lesson 4 counts how much this overlap shrinks the real sample.

quiz.prose: A model is trained on 20-day fixed-horizon labels with features from the past. Its author scores it with 5-fold cross-validation on shuffled rows and gets a 61% hit rate.
quiz.question: What is the main problem?

options.text: Test rows sit between training rows whose labels share 19 of their 20 days, so the answer leaks in
Five folds is too few for a stable estimate
options.why: More folds would not help. Shuffled folds put near-copies of each test label in training.

options.text: Nothing: cross-validation always gives an honest score
options.why: It is honest only when rows are independent. Validation lesson 5 showed shuffling a time series lies.

options.text: The classes may be unbalanced
options.why: Worth checking, but not the main problem. The folds leak the labels.

feedback.correct: Shuffled folds hand the model its neighbours' answers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what training rows sit next to each test row.

explain.text: With a 20-day label, the rows either side of a test row share 19 days of its outcome. Shuffling puts them in training, so the model is graded on answers it has nearly seen. Validation lessons 5 and 7 give the fix: time-ordered folds with a purge.

quiz.prose: Recent daily volatility is $\sigma = 1.2\%$. The label horizon is $h = 4$ days and $k = 0.5$. A four-day return of $+0.9\%$ arrives.
quiz.question: What is its label?

options.text: $0$: the bar is $0.5 \times 1.2\% \times 2 = 1.2\%$

options.why: You used the one-day bar. A four-day return spreads $\sqrt{4} = 2$ times wider.

options.text: $+1$: any rise is $+1$
options.why: That is the plain sign label. With a dead zone, small moves get $0$.

explain.text: The bar is $k\sigma\sqrt{h} = 0.5 \times 1.2\% \times 2 = 1.2\%$. A move of 0.9% is inside it, so the label is 0. The $\sqrt{h}$ is there because an $h$-day return spreads that much wider than one day.

quiz.prose: A feature is updated every day from yesterday's return. The label is the sign of the next 20 days' return. A colleague counts 1,000 daily rows as 1,000 independent tests of the feature.
quiz.question: Why is 1,000 too many?

options.text: The label changes slowly: each row shares 19 days of outcome with the next, so rows repeat one bet
The feature uses yesterday, so it is stale
options.why: A one-day lag is fine for a feature. The trouble is the 20-day label spanning many rows.

options.text: 1,000 is right: one row per day
options.why: Rows per day is not independent evidence. Neighbouring labels share 95% of their days.

feedback.correct: A label 20 times longer than the feature's step repeats the same outcome.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how often the feature changes with how often the label does.

explain.text: The feature changes daily but the label covers 20 days, so 20 neighbouring rows score almost the same outcome. The 1,000 rows hold far fewer independent bets. Lesson 4 measures how many.
